‘ “whosoever shall give you a cup of water to drink in my name, because ye belong to Christ,
verily I say unto you, he shall not lose his reward” ’ (Mark ix 41), whereas in Milton’s Comus
(ll. 523–29, 665–89) and Goethe’s Faust (ll. 690–741) it is clear that the attempts of Comus
and Mephistopheles respectively to persuade the Lady and Faust to drink are designed to
bring grave harm. The many sources at play in the final section are layered in such a manner
as to appear highly conventional while offering no clear way to read the ‘shape all light’, an
ambiguity which has led to numerous attempts to understand the figure and her behaviour
